INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici are three nonprofit entities who rely on the
challenged legislation to help Washington State youth
who are homeless or at risk of homelessness.  The
Skagit Valley Family YMCA operates the Oasis Youth
Shelter, an overnight shelter serving homeless and
runaway youth. This program can provide overnight
shelter to youth ages 13 –17 for up to 90 days, while
also providing case management focused on housing,
family reunification and natural supports, education
and employment, and connections to health care, including mental health, medical, and dental services.
Oasis Youth Shelter relies on Washington State’s
framework for protecting homeless youth —including
the legislation challenged in this lawsuit —on a regular basis to support youth who would otherwise have
few, if any, safe alternatives to sleeping on the streets.
TeamChild is a nationally recognized, nonprofit
civil legal aid organization providing similar legal aid
services to youth experiencing homelessness in Washington State. TeamChild’s mission is to uphold the
rights of youth involved or at risk of involvemen t in
the juvenile legal system to help them secure the education, health care, housing, and other support they
need to achieve positive outcomes in their lives.
TeamChild draws on multiple strategies to advance
this mission with an emphasis on direct repre sent-

TeamChild has participated as amicus in many cases
to advocate for youth in Washington State and nationally.
Similarly, the mission of Legal Counsel for Youth
and Children (LCYC) is to protect the interests and
safety of youth in Washington by advancing their legal rights, including through providing free civil legal
services to young people who are experiencing or at
risk of housing instability.  LCYC operates on the
premise that young people are neither the possessions
of parents nor of the State. One critical way in which
LCYC effects its mission is its Youth Homeless Programs. Young people aged 12–24 who are experiencing or at risk of housing instability can be eligible for
LCYC’s free civil legal services. Young people served
through this program include not just those experiencing homelessness but those who are on the median:
couch surfing, struggling to access emergency shelter,
temporarily living with friends or family, facing eviction, or feeling unsafe or unwelcome at home.  It is
these youth whose interests are protected by the legislation petitioners challenge in this lawsuit.
Thus, amici are uniquely positioned to explain why
the challenged legislation protects homeless youth,
rather than harms parents, and thus imposes no injury on petitioners that could bestow Article III standing.

INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
No parent is “targeted,” Brief for Petitioners 1, by
this legislation, which is about protecting homeless
youth, not limiting parental rights.  The two enactments at issue, Substitute House Bill 1406 (SHB 1406)
and Engrossed Substitute Senate Bill 5599 (ESSB
5599), combat the risk of hom elessness among youth
and children, including those who are seeking or receiving gender -affirming health care. 2 To be sure,
the question how best to protect youth at risk of homelessness is a critical one, and amici  acknowledge the
vital interest that parents have in its resolution. But
the challenged legislation poses no threat to that interest, which Washington State parents including petitioners have abundant opportunity to express
through the democratic process. Instead, petitioners’
theory of injury rests on false legal conclusions that
are divorced from the statutory text and that this
Court need not credit. See Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U. S.
662, 678 (2009) (“[T]he tenet that a court must accept
as true all of the allegations contained in a complaint
is inapplicable to legal conclusions.”).
Correcting these legal misapprehensions demonstrates that the challenged laws impose no redressable injury that could confer Article III standing on petitioners, for four reasons.  First, SHB 1406 simply
closes a legislative loophole that denied homeless
youth shelter access —keeping them on the streets
——————
2 Annotated copies of SHB 1406 and ESSB 5599 are included
as Appendix A hereto.

4 INTERNATIONAL PARTNERS FOR
ETHICAL CARE, INC. v. FERGUSON

needlessly—because youth previously lacked the legal
power to consent to a shelter’s caring for them.  Fixing this injures no one.
Second, injury is likewise absent from ESSB 5599
which, far from concealing children from their parents,
promotes family reconciliation.  ESSB 5599 adjusts
how—not whether—parents receive notice that their
child reported to a shelter, by mandating that such
notice be provided through the Washington State Department of Children, Youth, and Families (Department), which must make affirmative efforts to reconcile those parents with their children.  This serves
the goal petitioners claim to champion: healing the
breach between runaway children and their parents.
Third, because this legislation promotes family reconciliation, it is unsurprising that these modest
changes accomplish none of the parade of horribles petitioners allege. No person or entity can “get custody,”
App. to Pet. for Cert. 72a (¶  20), of any child under
these laws. No shelter or doctor is authorized to “facilitate a gender transition,” Brief for Petitioners 3,
without parental consent. No child is concealed from
their parents. No parent is compelled to use particular pronoun s. And, most critically: no homeless
youth is sent down the arduous road towards termination of parental rights—a remedy of last resort that
is governed by an entirely discrete statutory scheme
untethered from the challenged legislation. Petitioners’ “Sword of Damocles,” Brief for Petitioners 2, is imaginary.
Fourth, because no Sword of Damocles exists, a ruling for petitioners would redress none of the harm

as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents

they claim, which derives from the actions of persons
other than respondents who operate outside the auspices of the challenged legislation. Petitioners blame
everyone from school counselors to family friends for
the breakdown in their relationship with th eir children. App. to Pet. for Cert. 69a–77a. But no petitioner alleges that a youth shelter or any other entity
governed by this legislation played a role in that
breakdown. Thus, striking down this legislation
would not stop petitioners’ children from di sagreeing
with them about gender or from running away.  It
would only harm homeless youth.
Therefore, as detailed herein, the Ninth Circuit correctly affirmed the district court’s finding that petitioners lack Article III standing.  This Court should
affirm the Ninth Circuit.
ARGUMENT
I. Petitioners F undamentally Misconstrue
the Challenged Legislation
A. Washington State law recognizes the
rights of youth, the importance of
combatting youth homelessness, and
the primacy of family reunification.
1. This Court must give effect to
youth and children’s fundamental
rights.
“Children are no longer considered property.”
Anne C. Dailey and Laura A. Rosenbury, The New
Law of the Child, 127 Yale L. J. 1448, 1460 (Apr. 2018).
While the primacy of a parent’s authority over their

6 INTERNATIONAL PARTNERS FOR
ETHICAL CARE, INC. v. FERGUSON
Brief of the Skagit Valley Family YMCA, et al.,
as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
child forms the crux of the petitioners’ case, they overlook that children, as well as parents, have well-established rights that the challenged legislation protects.
Youth and children “are ‘persons’ under our Constitution.” Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community
School Dist., 393 U. S. 503, 511 (1969). They are entitled to constitutional protections.  See In re Gault,
387 U.  S. 1, 13 (1967) (explaining that “neither the
Fourteenth Amendment nor the Bill of Rights is for
adults alone.”) (citations omitted).  While they may
have their rights curtailed by their parents or the
State, “recognition of children’s autonomy comes into
play most often with respect to adolescent decision
making outside of the home.” Dailey and Rosenbury,
at 1461. 3 Thus, Washington State recognizes that
youth have a fundamental right to “conditions of basic
nurture” as well as “physical and mental health, and
safety.” Wash.  Rev. Code §  13.34.020. These rights
give Washington State a powerful interest in protecting youth from homelessness, as the following section
demonstrates.
——————
3  Indeed, the “muddled” nature of the line between a young
child in need of firm guidance and an adolescent capable of adult
decision-making, Dailey and Rosenbury, at 1465, is one reason
legislatures, rather than federal courts, are best suited to tackle
thorny questions about adolescent decision -making outside the
home. See also id., at 1466 (“In fact, the variable age of adulthood often reflects social and political considerations other than,
or in addition to, assumptions about children’s capacity for autonomous decision making.  This was evident when the voting
age was reduced to t he draft age during the Vietnam War era,
and it is evident now when some states prosecute children as
adults while other states do not.”).

2. The Court should take cognizance
of the State’s interest—shared by
Amici—in combatting youth
homelessness.
The need to protect homeless youth is acute.
Simply put, appalling things happen to children living
on the streets. As amici know firsthand, the risk of
harm to homeless youth is concrete and forms the core
of the Washington State Legislature’s declaration of
intent in creating the Office of Homeless Youth Prevention and Protection Programs:
“This population is exposed to an increased level
of violence, human trafficking, and exploitation
resulting in a higher incidence of substance abuse,
illness, and death.  The prevention and reduction of youth and young adult homelessness and
protection of homeless youth is of key concer n to
the state.” Wash. Rev. Code § 43.330.700(1).
Thus, Washington State has made a legal commitment to protect the health and safety of youth.  The
State effects that commitment not only by protecting
homeless youth but also by seeking to reunite them
with their parents, as described below.
3. The family unit’s primacy is wellrecognized throughout Washington
State’s legal framework for
combatting youth homelessness.
Petitioners posture this litigation as a defense of the
family unit, but that interest already permeates the
statutory scheme protecting the rights of youth and

Brief of the Skagit Valley Family YMCA, et al.,

children and is unthreatened by the challenged legislation. The statutory provisions protecting youth at
issue here include:
• the Family Reconciliation Act (codified at
Wash. Rev. Code, ch. 13.32A);
• the Homeless Housing and Assistance Act (codified at Wash. Rev. Code, ch. 43.185C);
• the Homeless Youth Prevention and Protection
Act (codified at Wash.  Rev. Code §§ 43.330.700–
43.330.726); and
• Wash. Rev. Code, ch. 74.15, “Care of Children,
Expectant Mothers, Persons with Developmental Disabilities.
These are the statutory provisions amended by the
bills petitioners challenge, SHB 1406 and ESSB 5599.
This carefully integrated statutory scheme balances
preventing youth homelessness, protecting parental
rights, and safeguarding the family unit by reuniting
homeless youth with their parents:
• The Family Reconciliation Act presumes that
“the experience and maturity of parents make
them better qualified to establish guidelines
beneficial to and protective of their children.”
Wash. Rev. Code §  13.32A.010. That Act requires parents be notified and family reconciliation services be offered “as soon as possible,” and
no later than three days, after youth report to a
shelter. Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082.
• The Homeless Housing and Assistance Act imposes a “[d]uty to inform parents” when crisis
residential shelters admit homeless children.
Wash. Rev. Code § 43.185C.280.

• The Homeless Youth Prevention and Protection
Act reflects the Legislature’s intent to prioritize
“family reconciliation” when supporting homeless youth, leaving dependency ( i. e., the first
step in the long process that might conclude with
terminating parental rights, see infra, Part I.D)
as a last resort when reconciliation is not viable.
Wash. Rev. Code § 43.330.700(1).4
• Wash. Rev. Code § 74.15.020(2)(o)(ii)(A) compels
the Department to make a good faith attempt to
notify the parent of any child seeking or receiving protected health care services at a host home
program within 72 hours.
Thus, the statutory scheme protects petitioners’ interests as parents. None of the foregoing is imperiled
by the challenged legislation, discussed below.
B. SHB 1406 fixes a legislative flaw
needlessly keeping youth on streets.
Youth, not parents, are the “objects of the laws at
issue,” Brief for Petitioners i, here.  SHB 1406 has
one focus: getting youth off streets and into shelters.
Previously, the Family Reconciliation Act contained a
loophole denying some youth shelter access even when
their parents refused to permit them to return home.5
When a youth sought assistance from a homeless

back to the streets —unless it could obtain the parent’s6 affirmative consent to the youth remaining in
the shelter.  That is because the version of
Wash. Rev. Code §  13.32A.082 effective before SHB
1406 contained no provision allowing youth to directly
authorize shelters to help them —only the parents
could provide that consent. See App. to Br. of Skagit
YMCA, et al. 4 (SHB 1406 at 2:34– 35, adding youth
consent language to pre -amendment statute).  The
absence of such a provision might even have caused
shelters to fear criminal liability for unlawful harboring of a minor had they permitted the youth to remain
without parental consent.  See Wash. Rev. Code
§ 13.32A.080(1)(a) (criminalizing unlawful harboring
of a minor).
Thus, previously, a shelter could not help a homeless child if the shelter could not make contact with
their parents ( e. g., the parents do not return phone
calls or their phone number is disconnected). And, if
the shelter did make contact, the parents could refuse
consent for the youth to stay at the shelter while also
refusing to permit the youth to return home.  Either
way, the youth remained on the streets.  In that
event, the shelter had few options to help them.  It
could contact the police to request they take the minor
into protective custody under Wash.  Rev. Code
§ 26.44.050. But that would require grounds to report abuse or neglect. Ibid. And this could start the

youth down the arduous road to a dependency petition

SHB 1406 closes this loophole.  As amended,
Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082(1)(b)(i) provides: “A minor may provide authorization to remain” in a shelter
for up to 90 days if the parents cannot be contacted or
refuse to permit the youth to come home.
App. to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 4 –5 (SHB 1406 at
2:34–3:12). When that happens, the shelter must notify the Department, which must contact the parents
and seek to reconcile the family. App. to Br. of Skagit
YMCA, et al. 6 (SHB 1406 at 3:36– 4:4).7 That must
occur “as soon as possible” and, at the latest, within
“three days, excluding weekends and holidays.” App.
to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 6.  This emphasis on
prompt parental notice also appears throughout the
second component of the challenged legislation, discussed below.

C. ESSB 5599 promotes reconciliation
among parents and youth seeking
gender-related health care by adjusting
how—not whether—parents receive
notice their child reported to a shelter.
ESSB 5599 is about the manner of parental notice,
not whether notice occurs.  In enacting ESSB 5599,
the Washington State Legislature recognized the
heightened health and safety risk of homelessness afflicting transgender youth.  App. to Br. of Skagit
YMCA, et al. 18 (ESSB 5599 at 1:5 –16). Similar to
SHB 1406, ESSB 5599 solves this problem primarily
by mandating the Department seek to reconcile these
youth with their family when the youth present at a
shelter or host home program.
Parental notice forms the core of this framework.
The Family Reconciliation Act mandates a shelter
serving youth promptly notify the parents. Wash. Rev.
Code §  13.32A.082(1)(b)(i). If the shelter has “compelling reasons” not to notify the parents directly, it
instead notifies the Department. Ibid. The Department must then notify the parent “as soon as possible”
and work to reunify the youth with their parents. Id.,
§ 13.32A.082(3)(a).
ESSB 5599’s only material change is to effect notice
through the Department rather than through shelters.
Addressing the increased likelihood of homelessness
among transgender youth “seeking or receiving . . .
gender affirming treatment . . . ” 8 —and the
——————
8 App. to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 18 and App.  to Br. of Skagit
YMCA, et al. 20–21 (ESSB 5599, pp. 1 and 3).

commensurate increased risk of harm to those youth
if they remain on the streets—ESSB 5599 makes that
status a “compelling reason” for the shelter or host
home to notify the parents of their child’s whereabouts
through the Department rather than directly. App. to
Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 20 (ESSB 5599 at 3:1 –10,
amending Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082(2)(c)). And,
if the youth seeks gender -affirming health care, the
Department must “offer”—not compel or coerce—for
the youth to connect to providers of appropriate “behavioral”—not medical —health services. App.  to Br.
of Skagit YMCA, et al. 21 (ESSB 5599 at 3:15 –19).
See also infra, Part II.C.2 (explaining absence of any
provision permitting youth to undergo medical treatment without parental consent).
And the parents still receive the same notice they
would otherwise have received.  ESSB 5599 makes
notice mandatory: the Department “shall make a good
faith attempt to notify the parent.” App.  to Br. of
Skagit YMCA, et al. 28 (ESSB 5599 at 8:10– 13) (emphasis added). See also App.  to Br. of Skagit YMCA,
et al. 6 (SHB 1406 at 3:36– 4:4, retaining pre -amendment language requiring parental notice). Thus, parental notice was the law before ESSB 5599 and remains the law post-amendment.
The only change ESSB 5599 accomplishes is mandating that notice include efforts at family reunification, provided through the Department.  Now, when
the Department notifies parents that their child presented at a shelter, ESSB 5599 requires that the Department also “offer services designed to resolve the
conflict and accomplish a reunification of the family.”

App. to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 28 (ESSB 5599 at
8:12–13). See also App.  to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al.
21 (ESSB 5599 at 3:20–21, requiring the Department
to “offer services designed to resolve the conflict and
accomplish a reunification of the family”).  This promotes the State’s and the children’s interest in maintaining the integrity of the family unit by enabling the
Department, which is better equipped than shelters to
effect reunification, to work to reconcile the youth
with their parents.
That is the long and the short of it.  No parent is
deprived of notice under ESSB 5599. No child is concealed from their parents. And ESSB 5599 provides
no mechanism for the State to take custody of a youth
or curtail a parent’s rights if they decline to recognize
their child’s preferred gender identity (the one and
only mechanism for accomplishing this solution of last
resort remains a dependency petition, as discussed below).
D. Neither SHB 1406 nor ESSB 5599
permits the State to obtain legal
custody of youth or terminate parental
rights.
Petitioners face no “loss of custody,” Brief for Petitioners 52. No provision of SHB 1406 or ESSB 5599
permits the State to terminate a parent’s rights concerning or relationship with their child.  These
amendments take not one step down the long road to
that outcome. That remains the sole province of the
Juvenile Court Act, Wash. Rev. Code, ch. 13.34. Captioned “Dependency and Termination of Parent-Child
Relationship,” that Act provides the mechanism by

which the State may take custody of youth. 9 And,
while that mechanism is divorced from the changes
SHB 1406 and ESSB 5599 accomplish and is not challenged in this lawsuit, it is notable that dependency
contains numerous procedural safeguards and is
founded on the State’s recognition that “the family
unit is a fundamental resource of American life [which]
should remain intact unless a child’s right to conditions of basic nurture, health, or safety is jeopardized.”
Wash. Rev. Code §  13.34.020. No one’s parental
rights are at risk under the challenged legislation.
E. The fears animating petitioners’
lawsuit are absent.
Because the statutory text before the Court says
nothing about terminating parental rights, concealing
children’s whereabouts from their parents, or compelling youth to seek gender -affirming health care, it is
unsurprising that they have little correlation  to the
allegations of petitioners’ First Amended Complaint
(App. to Pet. for Cert. 66a–139a). The following allegations find no basis in the challenged legislation:
• Nothing about this legislation “prevents or delays notice to parents of runaway children” (App.
to Pet. for Cert. 67a (¶ 3));
• Nothing requires the State to “promote ‘gender
transitions’” (App. to Pet. for Cert. 68a (¶ 4));10

ledge” (App. to Pet. for Cert. 68a (¶ 6));
• Nothing applies differently to “certain parents—
but not all parents” ( App. to Pet. for Cert. 68a
(¶ 8));
• Nothing treats “a parent’s refusal to ‘affirm’ a
child’s gender dysphoria” as “abuse or neglect”
(App. to Pet. for Cert. 81a–82a (¶ 81));
• Nothing removes the “time period for notifying
parents” when their child presents to a shelter
(App. to Pet. for Cert. 83a (¶ 84));
• Nothing “penalizes” parents who refer to their
children by particular pronouns (App. to Pet. for
Cert. 100a (¶ 129)); and
• Most fundamentally, nothing in the challenged
amendments intersects with existing law permitting minors to obtain health care to “emancipate[] children from parental control” ( App. to
Pet. for Cert. 92a (¶ 109)).

See also infra, Part II.C.2 (explaining that the Legislature’s
choice to use the term “appropriate behavioral health services”
(which does not include gender-affirming medical treatment) rather than the defined term “Protected health care services”
(which explicitly inc ludes “gender affirming treatment”) indicates that gender transitions are not offered to children under
the challenged legislation.)

The bottom line is Washington State parents remain free to oppose their child’s gender identity, urge
them not to express their gender, or refuse to provide
gender-affirming health care.  The challenged
amendments serve only to reduce the likelihood that
youth remain on the streets when conflicts over the
foregoing cause a rift in the family that ejects the child
from their home.
II. A Correct Understanding of the Challenged
Legislation Confirms that the Petitioners
Lack Article III Standing
A. Only injury—not policy preferences—
may clothe petitioners with Article III
standing.
Stripped of the misapprehensions detailed above,
the gist of petitioners’ case is their opposition to youth
homeless shelters such as amici  offering to refer
homeless youth for behavioral health services that petitioners oppose as a matter of general social policy.
But Article III of our Constitution prevents the petitioners from circumventing the democratic process by
asking a federal court to impose those policy preferences over the Legislature’s efforts to protect homeless youth. Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U. S. 330, 338
(2016) (citing Clapper v. Amnesty International USA,
568 U. S. 398, 408 (2013); Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U. S. 555, 576–577 (1992)). Amici concur in
the Ninth Circuit’s conclusion that the petitioners
lack Article III standing because they cannot show the
challenged legislation inflicts redressable harm.

ETHICAL CARE, INC. v. FERGUSON
Brief of the Skagit Valley Family YMCA, et al.,
as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
To show harm and thereby establish “injury in fact,”
the first and foremost element of this Court’s test for
Article III standing, petitioners must plead that they
have “personally” “suffered some actual or threatened
injury” that is “concrete and particularized,” not “conjectural or hypothetical.” Spokeo, 578 U.  S., at 338–
339 (citing Steel Co. v. Citizens for Better Environment,
523 U. S. 83, 103 (1998), Valley Forge Christian College v. Americans United for Separation of Church and
State, Inc., 454 U.  S. 464, 472 (1982), and Lujan, 504
U. S., at 560).  That means petitioners must plead
that SHB 1406 and ESSB 5599 hurt them “in a personal and individual way.” Spokeo, 578 U. S., at 339
(collecting cases). That injury must “actually exist.”
Spokeo, 578 U. S., at 340 (citing Black’s Law Dictionary 506 (10th ed. 2014)).
Petitioners must further demonstrate that a federal
court could remedy their supposed injury.  See
Spokeo, 578 U. S., at 338 (an injury conferring Article
III standing must be “likely to be redressed by a favorable judicial decision.”) (citations omitted).  Specifically, they must plead that the claimed injury can be
redressed by a ruling against the Washingto n State
officials they sue. See, e. g., Lujan, 504 U. S., at 568–
570 (redressability element of Article III standing was
unmet where a ruling against the defendant would
not apply to other government agencies who were not
parties to the suit and would not be bound by any
judgment).
Correcting petitioners’ misunderstanding of the
challenged legislation demonstrates they plead no redressable injury, as explained below.

as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents

B. No plaintiff alleges injury from SHB
1406’s permitting youth to consent to
shelter access when the parents cannot
be reached or refuse to consent while
simultaneously refusing to permit the
child to return home.
To establish injury in fact, petitioners would have
to plead they fall within the narrow loophole SHB
1406 closes. As detailed supra, Part I.B, SHB 1406
allows youth to consent to stay in shelters when their
parents cannot be reached or will not consent to shelter but refuse to permit the child to return home.
This reduces the likelihood the State brings a dependency petition while increasing the likelihood that the
youth has a safe place to stay while the family works
toward reunification. Contrary to petitioners’ implication, the challenged amendments do not seek to estrange youth receiving gender-related health care services from their parents, but rather recognize the estrangement that disagreements about such fundamental matters as gender identity or fa ith can inflict
on the family unit and put the Department in a position to heal the breach.
No petitioner alleges this harms them. Petitioners
claim the challenged legislation might permit their
children to receive gender- affirming care without
their notice or consent.  Brief for Petitioners 8 –18.
But no petitioner alleges facts supporting a reaso nable inference that, if their child were to run away and
present to a shelter, either (a) the shelter would be
unable to contact them or (b) they would refuse consent for their child to remain in the shelter while also

ETHICAL CARE, INC. v. FERGUSON
Brief of the Skagit Valley Family YMCA, et al.,
as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
refusing to permit the child to return home. Without
these allegations, the petitioners simply do not fall
within SHB 1406’s narrow arc.
C. No plaintiff alleges injury from ESSB
5599’s parental notice mechanism.
Petitioners identify five categories of harm from
ESSB 5599’s changing the manner of notice from provision by shelters to provision by the Department.
As explained below, each supposes a legal strawman
the Court need not credit.  See Iqbal, 556 U.  S., at
678 (“the tenet that a court must accept as true all of
the allegations contained in a complaint is inapplicable to legal conclusions.”).
1. Parents receive prompt notice.
Petitioners’ claim that the legislation strips them of
previous protections by depriving them of notice, Brief
for Petitioners 8–9, is incorrect. ESSB 5599 changes
the mechanism of notice only. When a shelter or host
home notifies the Department that a chi ld seeking
protected health care services has arrived, the Department must notify the parents and seek to accomplish
family reunification “as soon as possible.”
App. to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 21 (ESSB 5599 at
3:11–14) and App.  to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 6
(SHB 1406 at 3:36 –4:4). That must occur “no later
than three days, excluding weekends and holidays,”
following the receipt of a report that the child presented at the shelter. App. to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al.
6 (SHB 1406 at 4:1– 4). No statutory tex t supports
petitioners’ reading.

Brief of the Skagit Valley Family YMCA, et al.,
as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents

To the contrary, petitioners themselves
acknowledge—and the Court may rely on this allegation when reviewing an order granting a motion to dismiss—that the Department interprets ESSB 5599 to
require parental notice where the youth presenting to
a shelter seeks protected health care services.
App. to Pet. for Cert. 86a (¶ 93) (pleading department
implements ESSB 5599 to require parental notification); Branch v. Tunnell, 14 F. 3d 449, 453 (CA9 1994)
(citations omitted) (ruling court may consider documents referred to in a complaint on a motion to dismiss). This confirms that petitioners’ claimed injury
is nonexistent.  See Taylor v. Burlington N. R.  R.
Holdings, Inc., 444 P. 3d 606, 614 (Wash. 2019) (citations omitted) (stating agency’s interpretation of a
statute it is charged with administering is highly persuasive).
2. Children do not receive genderrelated health care merely by
reporting to a shelter.
Petitioners say they are shut out from their child’s
health care decisions because, if their child ran away
and presented at a shelter, the Department would offer to refer the child to appropriate behavioral health
services which, petitioners suppose, means their child
might undergo gender transition surgery without
their consent.  Brief for Petitioners 9 –12. Four
items demonstrate this theory’s implausibility.
First and foremost: no provision of the challenged
legislation permits youth to undergo medical treatment without parental consent. Although a separate
and long -standing statute, Wash.  Rev. Code

ETHICAL CARE, INC. v. FERGUSON

as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
§ 71.34.530, permits adolescents to receive behavioral
health services without parental consent, no corresponding provision permits youth to receive gender -
affirming medical care without parental consent. 11
Notably, this chapter is captioned “Behavioral Health
Services for Minors” and says nothing of medical care.
Wash. Rev. Code, ch. 71.34.  See also Wash.  Rev.
Code §§  71.34.010 (describing statutory purpose in
terms of “behavioral” care) and 71.34.020 (omitting
gender-affirming treatment from definitions).  Petitioners identify nothing in the challenged legislation
expanding this provision to permit youth to acce ss
gender-affirming medical care without parental consent. This Court should not imply it where none exists.
Second, given the foregoing, petitioners’ conclusory
supposition that gender transitions could be accomplished “merely by taking the children to a shelter,”
Brief for Petitioners 17, finds no support in the statutory text or in petitioners’ factual allegat ions. This
allegation thus merits rejection. See Iqbal, 556 U. S.,
at 681 (“It is the conclusory nature of respondent’s allegations, rather than their extravagantly fanciful nature, that disentitles them to the presumption of
truth.”). Youth homeless shelters do not perform
surgery. Nor do they offer other medical care such as
hormones or other gender-affirming treatment.
Third, the statutory term “appropriate behavioral
health services” does not mean, as petitioners say,

where parental consent was absent.

“gender transitions,” Brief for Petitioners i. Elementary statutory construction debunks petitioners’ misreading. The words “gender transition” are absent
from the challenged legislation; puberty blockers, hormones, or surgery appear nowhere. App.  to Br. of
Skagit YMCA, et al. 1 –31. See Barnhart v. Sigmon
Coal Co., 534 U. S. 438, 450 (2002) (citations omitted)
(“[a]s in all statutory construction cases, we begin
with the language of the statute . . . .  The inquiry
ceases ‘if the statutory language is unambi guous . . . .’”). These terms’ absence is striking because
the Washington State Legislature includes them elsewhere. The term “protected health care services” explicitly includes “gender affirming treatment.”
App. to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 20 (ESSB 5599 at
3:8–10). Thus, had the Legislature intended the Department to refer youth for “gender transitions” as petitioners misapprehend, it would have required referral for “protected health care services” rather than
“appropriate behavioral health services.” The Legislature’s decision to use separate terms controls.  See
Ysleta Del Sur Pueblo v.  Texas, 596 U.  S. 685, 698
(2022) (“differences in language like this convey differences in meaning”) (quotation omitted).
Fourth, the supposition that a child might undergo
gender-affirming medical care before their parents receive notice defies common sense.  See Iqbal, 556
U. S., at 679 (“[D]etermining whether a complaint
states a plausible claim . . . requir[es] the reviewing
court to draw on its experience and common sense.”)
(citation omitted) . Petitioners invite the Court to
suppose that a convoluted chain of hypotheticals can

as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
occur within the 72 hours in which the law mandates
the parents receive notice so that they may reconcile
with their child:
• a petitioner’s child presents to a shelter (even
though no petitioner alleges this has happened
or is about to happen);
• the shelter refers the child for gender -affirming
surgery or hormones (even though the challenged legislation does not tell them to);
• the child connects with a qualified provider;
• the provider obtains the child’s complete medical
history;
• the provider evaluates the child and opines that
surgery or hormones are medically necessary;
• billing and insurance coverage are negotiated;
and
• the provider performs the procedure without parental consent (risking criminal prosecution under Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.080(1)(a)).
The assertion that this could all occur within 72
hours flunks the Fed.  Rule Civ. Proc. 8(a) pleading
standard. See, e.  g., Hikma Pharmaceuticals USA
Inc. v. Amarin Pharma, Inc., 608 U. S. 580, 595 (2026)
(finding complaint failed to state a claim based on attenuated chain of hypothetical events; “Perhaps this
chain of events is ‘possib[le]’ (anything is possible) . . . .
[b]ut, without more, it is not a ‘“plausible”’ scenario . . .
giving rise to liability . . . .”) (citations omitted).

as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents

3. Notice through the Department is
not an injury.
Petitioners’ contention that they are harmed because shelters are “forbidden to notify parents,” Brief
for Petitioners 12, misreads the legislation in a manner the Court need not credit. Iqbal, 556 U. S., at 678.
Far from forbidding notice, ESSB 5599 mandates it,
through the Department, for the express purpose of
healing intrafamily conflict and reuniting children
with their parents. Supra, Part I.C. Petitioners speculate that their child might thwart the Department’s
providing notice by withholding their parents’ contact
information. Brief for Petitioners 7.  Not only is
this too vague to make out a plausible theory of injury,
that injury could not be redressed by a ruling in petitioners’ favor; even if ESSB 5599 were struck down
and shelters resumed providi ng notice to parents directly, rather than through the Department, a shelter
still could not provide notice to the parents if the child
withheld their contact information, leaving petitioners in the same position they presently complain of.
Spokeo, 578 U. S., at 338 (citation omitted). See infra,
Part II.E (explaining petitioners fail to plead any injury is redressable).  This emphasizes the central
flaw in petitioners’ theory of injury: ESSB 5599 is
about the manner of notice, not whether notice is provided.
4. Nothing denies parents
information about their child.
“[P]arents cannot reunite with their child even if
they receive notice,” argue petitioners, because, they

26 INTERNATIONAL PARTNERS FOR
ETHICAL CARE, INC. v. FERGUSON
Brief of the Skagit Valley Family YMCA, et al.,
as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
say, ESSB 5599 does not explicitly require the Department to disclose the child’s location or condition.
Brief for Petitioners 14. The statutory text discloses
otherwise. When the Department notifies parents
that their child presented at a shelter, the sta tute
states it “shall” offer services designed to “accomplish
a reunification of the family.”
App. to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 21 (ESSB 5599 at
3:11–14). That requirement applies expressly to
children seeking gender-affirming medical treatment.
App. to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 21 (ESSB 5599 at
3:15–21). The Court should give this unambiguous
language its plain meaning. See Barnhart, 534 U. S.,
at 450 (“[a]s in all statutory construction cases, we
begin with the language of the statute . . . .  The inquiry ceases ‘if the statutory language is unambiguous . . . .’”) (citations omitted).
Thus, because courts presume the Legislature
meant what it said by “accomplish a reunification of
the family,” that language cannot be read to permit
the Department to conceal children from their parents.
See Mullin v. Doe, 609 U.  S. 324, 342 (2026) (“Statutory interpretation proceeds on the assumption that
those who draft and enact a provision generally intend
its terms to mean what they mean in ordinary usage.”);
St. Martin Evangelical Lutheran Church v. South Dakota, 451 U. S. 772, 780 (1981) (“[a] statute, of course,
is to be construed, if such a construction is fairly possible, to avoid raising doubts of its constitutionality”)
(citations omitted). Petitioners cannot rewrite “reunify the family” to mean “conceal the child from their
parents.”

as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents

5. Nothing about ESSB 5599 delays
children’s return home.
Petitioners say this legislation permits the Department to delay reunifying children with their parents
indefinitely for the purpose of “entrenching” gender -
affirming treatment. Brief for Petitioners 14. Failing to identify statutory language reflecting th is (for
the excellent reason that there is none), petitioners resort to manufacturing ambiguity: they say that there
is no deadline for reunification to be accomplished, despite acknowledging the State’s interpretation that
the family must receive contact within 24 hours, thus
supposing “reunification is not required.” Id., at 14–
15. Reading a statute mandating “a reunification of
the family” to mean that reunification is not required
improperly ignores the statute’s plain language.
Mullin, 609 U. S., at 342.
D. This legislation threatens no one’s
parental rights.
It bears repeating: nothing in the challenged legislation threatens termination of parental rights. This
legislation imposes no requirement that parents recognize a child’s gender identity, use preferred pronouns, or take any other action as a precondition of
the Department’s seeking to reunite the family.
App. to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 1 –31; supra, Part
I.E. Nor does it even mention termination of parental
rights, which remains subject to a separate set of legislation, Wash. Rev. Code, ch. 13.34. Supra, Part I.D.
The challenged amendments leave those provisions
intact. Fear of harm from a hypothetical dependency

ETHICAL CARE, INC. v. FERGUSON
Brief of the Skagit Valley Family YMCA, et al.,
as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
proceeding under Wash.  Rev. Code, ch. 13.34 cannot
establish standing to challenge ESSB 5599.  See
Spokeo, 578 U. S., at 338 (an injury sufficient to confer
Article III standing must be “fairly traceable to the
challenged conduct of the defendant”) (citation omitted).
E. No federal court can redress the fears
animating this lawsuit.
Even if petitioners plead a cognizable injury, they
cannot show that injury could be redressed by a ruling
in their favor.  Spokeo, 578 U . S., at 338 (an injury
conferring Article III standing must be “likely to be
redressed by a favorable judicial decision.”) (citation
omitted). Petitioners’ case boils down to the proposition that the challenged legislation harms them by encouraging their ch ildren to run away from home in
pursuit of a gender identity they dispute.  Brief for
Petitioners 2. But petitioners attribute this injury to
a multitude of third parties besides respondents and
the homeless shelters who, like amici, are empowered
to help homeless youth under ESSB 5599 and SHB
1406. Petitioners blame their children’s recalcitrance on, variously, the “school district,” “a school
counselor,” “other school staff,” “school activities,” and
other children at school includ ing “bullies”
(App. to Pet. for Cert. 70a (¶¶  13–14),
App. to Pet. for Cert. 74a (¶¶  35 and 37),
App. to Pet. for Cert. 76a (¶  45), and
App. to Pet. for Cert. 77a (¶¶  52 and 57)); “friends,”
“other adults” or “a family of a friend”
(App. to Pet. for Cert. 74a (¶¶  34 and 36) and
App. to Pet. for Cert. 71a (¶  17)); “therapists and

Cite as: Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 29
Brief of the Skagit Valley Family YMCA, et al.,
as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents

behavioral health specialists” ( App. to Pet. for Cert.
77a (¶ 57)); an “older sister” (App. to Pet. for Cert. 72a
(¶ 24)); and “a popular tech platform”
(App. to Pet. for Cert. 73a (¶  25)). None of these are
creatures of the challenged legislation.
Thus, a ruling striking down this legislation could
not solve the familial disputes at the core of petitioners’ claimed injury.  See, e.  g., Lujan , 504 U.  S., at
568–570 (redressability element of Article III standing was unmet where a ruling against the defendant
would not apply to non-parties who were participants
in the alleged injury). Indeed, petitioners plead their
children were recalcitrant b efore this legislation.
See, e. g., App. to Pet. for Cert. 77a (¶¶ 52–56) (alleging
child previously ran away from home after choosing to
identify as transgender).  An adolescent determined
to defy their parents over matters as personal and profound as faith or gender will still run away even if legislation helping shelters protect them is invalidated.
All that would change if petitioners receive a favorable judicial decision is that these runaway children
will enjoy fewer protections and face greater harms
attendant to living unsheltered.  The reluctance of
children seeking gender -affirming care to get o ff the
streets and into shelters was the Legislature’s chief
animus in passing this legislation.  See
App. to Br. of Skagit YMCA, et al. 18 (ESSB 5599 declaration of legislative findings: “[B]arriers to accessing
shelter can place a chilling effect on exist ing unsheltered homelessness and therefore create additional
risk and dangers for youth.”).  The outcome of a victory for petitioners would not be that the intrafamily

30 INTERNATIONAL PARTNERS FOR
ETHICAL CARE, INC. v. FERGUSON
Brief of the Skagit Valley Family YMCA, et al.,
as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
conflict reflected in their complaint would quiet —the
sole outcome would be youth on the streets rather
than in shelter.  The harm petitioners claim cannot
be redressed by a court ruling.
CONCLUSION
Amici urge the Court to prevent legislation protecting homeless children from becoming embroiled in a
societal dispute about gender and faith that belongs
at the ballot box rather than the courthouse.  Because petitioners allege no injury that a federal court
could redress, this Court should rule that they lack
standing, affirm the Ninth Circuit, and let petitioners
assert their opposition to free expression of gender
identity through the democratic process.
Respectfully submitted.

AN ACT Relating to supporting youth and young
adults seeking protected health care services; amending RCW 13.32A.082 and 74.15.020; and creating new
sections.
BE IT ENACTED BY THE LEGISLATURE OF
THE STATE OF WASHINGTON:
NEW SECTION.  Sec. 1.  The legislature finds
that unsheltered homelessness for youth poses a serious threat to their health and safety.  The Trevor
project has found that one in three transgender youth
report attempting suicide.  Homelessness amongst
transgender youth can further endanger an already
at-risk population. The legislature further finds that
barriers to accessing shelter can place a chilling effect
on exiting unsheltered homelessness and therefore
create additional risk and dangers for youth.  Youth
seeking certain medical services are especially at risk
and vulnerable. Therefore, the legislature intends to
remove barriers to accessing temporary, licensed shelter accommodations for youth seeking certain protected health care services.
